newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries sharply lower on hawkish Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries sharply lower on hawkish Greenspan.

text.p: The prices of Treasury securities closed sharply lower Wednesday following the hawkish testimony of Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.

Greenspan hinted that preemptive tightening may be warranted should the economy continue to show strong growth during his appearance before the Senate Banking Committee. He voiced concern about soaring stock prices and warned of rising wage and inflation pressures.
The 30-year bond closed 1-1/2 lower at 98-03/32 to yield 6.77 percent.

"The markets essentially have been caught off guard. What he said effectively is he's very, very serious about some of the things he and others have said in the past," said Hugh Johnson, economist at First Albany Corp. Issues the Federal Reserve will not stand idly by on include speculation in the stock market and higher wages and inflation.

The only thing a little surprising to Johnson was the FOMC's forecast of real gross domestic product rising 2.0 percent to 2.25 percent. "That's lower than most forecasts and implies the Fed is ready to tighten sooner and by more than most expect," Johnson said.

"The market is now in the process of pricing in a 25-basis-point increase in interest rates," Johnson said. Johnson continued to believe that the Fed would be able to hold off a tightening at its March meeting. "However, all bets are off for May," he said.

"He obviously raised the possibility of tightening and perhaps as soon as March. There's no question he was more hawkish, he took an incremental step relative to where he had been," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp. "A preemptive strike was not in the cards previously."
Platt said the Fed chairman really focused on inflation and didn't acknowledge any weakness in the economy that could slow its rate of growth.

"I still don't think he has enough evidence to raise rates in March, but he clearly has changed the probability of such an event happening. Before the market had none and today's indigestion was the market trying to figure out at what levels to price in a tightening," said David Orr, chief capital markets economist at First Union Corp.
Orr said Wednesday's testimony served as a reality check that the "nirvana we've had can't continue indefinitely."

However, Orr said Greenspan's comments had to be taken in perspective. "He's not seeing any serious threat of rapid inflation and he painted a very pointed contrast between 1997 and 1994. In 1994 the real fed funds rate was clearly incompatible with containing inflation, whereas today it may be high enough to allow continued non-inflationary growth," Orr said.

It was important to look as much at the conclusion at the end of Greenspan's formal testimony that prospects for U.S. the economy were "quite favorable" as it was his comments on inflation, Orr said. "Even I must admit that economic prospects are quite favorable," he said.
As might be expected, trading volume was very heavy throughout the session. According to GoxPX, about $113.2 billion had been traded by about 1600 EST/2100 GMT.
"All the gain came from the coupon sector," said a spokeswoman for GovPX. She said volume was about 24 percent above what it normally was on a Wednesday.
"Today really mirrored the first day of Greenspan's Humphrey-Hawkins testimony last year when trading volume totaled $115.4 billion," she said.
Trading was particularly heavy in the two-year sector, with more than $11 billion trading hands, GovPX said.
Treasury's sale Wednesday of $12.5 billion of five-year notes, coming in the wake of Greenspan's testimony, met with weak demand.
Three-month bill rates rose three basis points to 5.05 percent. Six-month bill rates were 10 basis points higher at 5.09 percent and year-bill rates were 11 basis points higher 5.31 percent.

Two-year notes ended down 9/32 at 99-22/32, yielding 6.04 percent. Five-year notes closed at 99-19/32, down 21/32, yielding 6.35 percent. Ten-year notes ended at 98-even, down 31/32 to yield 6.53 percent.
